summary: Two blind men follow Jesus calling Him Son of David, and He opens their eyes; then He frees a mute man, and the Pharisees credit the devil.
key_insight: The crowds said, “It was never seen like this in Israel!” The Pharisees saw the same miracle and said, “He casts out demons by the ruler of the demons.” Matthew closes his ten miracles of chapters 8–9 with this split: the same evidence, two opposite verdicts.
story: As Jesus left there, two blind men followed Him, crying out, “Son of David, have mercy on us!” They kept following, and when He had gone into the house, the blind men came to Him.

Jesus asked them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to Him, “Yes, Lord.” Then He touched their eyes, saying, “According to your faith let it be to you.” And their eyes were opened.
Jesus sternly warned them, “See that no one knows it.” But as soon as they had gone, they spread the news about Him in all that country.

As they were going out, people brought Jesus a man who was mute and demon-possessed. When the demon was cast out, the mute man spoke. The crowds marveled, saying, “It was never seen like this in Israel!” But the Pharisees said, “He casts out demons by the ruler of the demons.”

scene.label: “Son of David”
scene.text: God promised David a descendant whose throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:12–13), so “Son of David” was a royal title for the Messiah. These blind men are the first people in Matthew to call Jesus by the name Matthew opened his Gospel with (Matthew 1:1).

scene.label: Blindness
scene.text: Eye disease was common in the ancient world, and there was no cure. Many blind people lived by begging, often by the roadside or at the city gate.

scene.label: A promised sign
scene.text: Isaiah said that when God came to save His people, “the eyes of the blind shall be opened,” and “the tongue of the dumb” would sing (Isaiah 35:5–6). Sight and speech are the very gifts given here.

scene.label: The charge
scene.text: “The ruler of the demons” is Beelzebub, a name for Satan. The Pharisees could not deny the miracle, so they attacked its source. Matthew records the same charge in fuller form later, where Jesus answers it (Matthew 12:22–32).

witnesses.matthew: Only Matthew tells these two healings, and they complete the ten miracles he gathers in chapters 8–9. They prepare for Jesus’ answer to John the Baptist, “The blind see” and “the deaf hear” (Matthew 11:5), and for the split that follows: crowds amazed, Pharisees opposed.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the Son of David who opens blind eyes, as Isaiah promised, yet He will not be swept along by the title. He asks for faith in His power, and He acts with an authority His enemies can oppose but cannot deny.
seeing.living: Jesus asked the blind men a plain question before He touched them: “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” Their answer was two words, “Yes, Lord.” Faith does not need to be eloquent; it needs to rest on His ability and say so to Him.
seeing.ponder: What need have you stopped bringing to Jesus because, deep down, you doubt He is able?

preaching.big_idea: The same miracle can open eyes or harden hearts.
preaching.watch_for: Watch the movement from public to private and back: a cry in the street (9:27), a healing inside the house (9:28–30), and news spread through all that country in spite of His warning (9:31). The scene ends in public again, with the crowds’ wonder and the Pharisees’ charge side by side (9:33–34).
